title: Expiring Session Tokens
statement:
Build a store for login tokens that expire. Every token lives for ttl seconds after it was issued or last renewed.

  • TokenKeeper(ttl) creates an empty store.
  • issue(tokenId, now) creates a new token that expires at now + ttl. A tokenId is never issued twice.
  • renew(tokenId, now) pushes the token's expiry to now + ttl, but only if the token exists and is still live. Renewing an unknown or expired token does nothing.
  • countLive(now) returns how many tokens are live at time now.

A token that expires at time t is already dead at time t: expiry happens before any other action at that same moment. The now values strictly increase from one call to the next.

Tests are written as a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the store. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: Renewing "a" at 4 moves its expiry from 6 to 9. "b" expires at 7, so it is gone at 7 and renewing it at 8 does nothing. At 9 "a" expires too.
"y" was never issued. "x" expires at 5, and expiry wins over the renewal at that same moment.

hints: A map from token to expiry time handles issue and renew in O(1). The hard part is counting live tokens without scanning every token each time.
Every expiry is set to now + ttl, and now only grows. So the most recently issued or renewed token always has the latest expiry. What does that say about the order of expiries?

Keep tokens in a map that remembers order of last touch. On renew, remove and re-insert the token so it moves to the back. On count, drop dead tokens from the front until the front one is live; the map's size is the answer.

explain.intuition:
The straightforward store is a map from token to its expiry time. issue and renew are O(1), but countLive has to look at every token, which is slow when there are many calls.

The trick: every expiry is now + ttl with the same ttl, and now only grows. So if you keep tokens in the order they were last touched, their expiries are sorted. The dead ones are always a prefix at the front. Like the LRU cache, an insertion-ordered map (Map in JavaScript, OrderedDict in Python) gives that order for free: renew means delete and re-insert. Counting just trims dead tokens from the front and returns the size. Each token is trimmed once, so the total work is O(1) per call on average.
steps: Keep an insertion-ordered map from token id to expiry time.
Before any operation at time now, remove tokens from the front while their expiry is ≤ now.
issue: insert the token at the back with expiry now + ttl.
renew: if the token is still in the map, delete it and insert it again at the back with expiry now + ttl.
pitfalls: Treating a token as live at the exact moment it expires. Use expiry > now, not ≥.
Renewing a token that has already expired, which brings it back to life. Check the expiry, or prune first.
Updating the expiry in place without moving the token to the back. The front of the map is then no longer the earliest expiry, and pruning stops too early.

solutions.title: Map and full scan
solutions.idea: Store each token's expiry in a map. Count by checking every token.
solutions.time: O(1) for issue and renew, O(n) for countLive

solutions.title: Ordered map, trimmed from the front
solutions.idea: Expiries come out sorted when tokens are kept in order of last touch, so dead tokens always sit at the front and can be dropped there.

followups: Each token can have its own ttl. Why does the ordered map stop working, and what replaces it?
The store runs on several servers behind a load balancer. Where should the expiry check live?
